etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ruyne, ruine, from Old French ruine, from Latin ruīna (“overthrow, ruin”), from ruō (“I fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush”).

definitions.definition: (countable, sometimes in the plural) The remains of a destroyed or dilapidated construction, such as a house or castle.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The Veian and the Gabian towirs shall fall, / And one promiscuous ruin cover all; / Nor, after length of years, a stone betray / The place where once the very ruins lay.
The labour of a day will not build up a virtuous habit on the ruins of an old and vicious character.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Foreword”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: A canister of flour from the kitchen had been thrown at the looking-glass and lay like trampled snow over the remains of a decent blue suit with the lining ripped out which lay on top of the ruin of a plastic wardrobe.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Eden Prime:
quote.text: Dr. Manuel: No one is saved. The age of humanity is ended. Soon, only ruin and corpses will remain.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The state of being a ruin, destroyed or decayed.
(uncountable) Something that leads to serious trouble or destruction.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Youth and Age”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: The errors of young men are the ruin of business.

quote.citation: 1920, Mary Roberts Rinehart, Avery Hopwood, chapter I, in The Bat: A Novel from the Play (Dell Book; 241), New York, N.Y.: Dell Publishing Company, →OCLC, page 01:
quote.text: The Bat—they called him the Bat. […]. He […] played a lone hand, […]. Most lone wolves had a moll at any rate—women were their ruin—but if the Bat had a moll, not even the grapevine telegraph could locate her.

quote.citation: [1611?], Homer, “(please specify |book=I to XXIV)”, in Geo[rge] Chapman, transl., The Iliads of Homer Prince of Poets. […], London:  […]  Nathaniell Butter, →OCLC; republished as The Iliads of Homer, Prince of Poets, […], new edition, volume (please specify the book number), London: Charles Knight and Co., […], 1843, →OCLC:
quote.text: His ruin startled th’ other steeds.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: A change that destroys or defeats something; destruction; overthrow.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene i, page 2:
quote.text: Oh Portius, is there not some choſen Curſe,Some hidden Thunder in the Stores of Heav’n,Red with uncommon Wrath, to blaſt the ManWho owes his Greatneſs to his Country’s Ruin?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause the fiscal ruin of; to bankrupt or drive out of business.

quote.citation: 1881–1882, Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island, London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 14 November 1883, →OCLC:
quote.text: In one way, indeed, he bade fair to ruin us; for he kept on staying week after week, and at last month after month, so that all the money had been long exhausted...

definitions.definition: To destroy or render something no longer usable or operable.

quote.citation: 1857, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, The Golden Mile-Stone:
quote.text: By the fireside there are old men seated, / Seeing ruined cities in the ashes.

definitions.definition: To upset or overturn the plans or progress of, or to have a disastrous effect on something.
To make something less enjoyable or likeable.
To reveal the ending of (a story); to spoil.
(obsolete) To fall into a state of decay.

quote.citation: 1636, George Sandys, Paraphrase upon the Psalmes and upon the Hymnes dispersed throughout the Old and New Testaments:
quote.text: Though he his house of polisht marble build, / Yet shall it ruine like the Moth's fraile cell

definitions.definition: (transitive, historical) To seduce or debauch, and thus harm the social standing of.
